Flu shots cannot cause flu illness. They are made with inactivated virus or a single virus protein.
Misconceptions About Seasonal Flu and Flu Vaccines
Common flu shot side effects are minor: soreness, redness or swelling where the shot was given, and sometimes headache, fever, muscle aches, nausea or tiredness.
Key Facts About Seasonal Flu Vaccine
Fainting can happen after any shot, so providers may have people sit for about 15 minutes afterward to prevent an injury.
Preventing and Managing Adverse Reactions (General Best Practice Guidelines for Immunization)

Protection from a flu vaccine builds over about two weeks after the shot, while the body makes antibodies. Someone exposed to flu just before or during that time can get sick before the vaccine protects them.
Key Facts About Seasonal Flu Vaccine
In the United States, flu activity most often peaks between December and February.

Tdap helps protect against tetanus, diphtheria and whooping cough (pertussis). For whooping cough, adults who have never had Tdap should get a single dose. After that, adults get a Td or Tdap booster every 10 years, and Td covers only tetanus and diphtheria.
Diphtheria, Tetanus, and Pertussis Vaccination: Information for Health Care Providers
A health care professional's recommendation is the strongest predictor of whether a patient gets vaccinated.

In seasons when the vaccine matches the circulating flu viruses well, flu vaccination reduces the risk of a flu-related doctor's visit by 40 to 60 percent. How well it works varies from season to season.
Among people hospitalized with flu, those who got a flu vaccine were less likely to need ICU admission, a ventilator or organ support.
Flu and the common cold are caused by different viruses but share many symptoms, so a cold can be hard to tell apart from flu.
Getting a flu vaccine may also help protect the people around you who are more likely to get very sick with flu, like babies and young children, older adults and pregnant women.
Anyone can get flu, including healthy people, and serious problems from flu can happen to anyone.
Anyone who needs a whooping cough or flu vaccine should get it at least two weeks before meeting a new baby.
Preteens, teens and adults who will be around a new baby and have not already had a whooping cough booster, called Tdap, should get one.
For most people, September and October are good times to get a flu vaccine, and ideally everyone is vaccinated by the end of October.
While there are some exceptions, most vaccines can be given at the same visit.
Getting a Flu Vaccine and Other Recommended Vaccines at the Same Time
CDC recommends an RSV vaccine for everyone 75 and older. Someone who has already had one does not need another at this time.

For people 65 and older, CDC preferentially recommends one flu vaccine each season from three kinds: high-dose, recombinant or adjuvanted. Any one of them meets the recommendation. Studies suggest they are potentially more effective in that age group. If one is not available, a standard-dose flu vaccine should be given instead.
Flu and People 65 Years and Older
People 65 and older account for 70 to 85 percent of flu-related deaths and 50 to 70 percent of flu-related hospitalizations each flu season.
Adults 50 and older should get the recombinant shingles vaccine, 2 doses given 2 to 6 months apart. For someone who has had shingles before, it can help prevent it coming back.
About 1 in 3 people in the United States will get shingles in their lifetime, and the risk goes up with age.
The shingles vaccine may be given at the same time as other vaccines.

When two shots are given at one visit, each goes at a different site. For adults, one deltoid muscle can take more than one shot, so both can go in the same arm if the patient prefers, at separate sites about an inch or more apart.
Vaccine Administration (General Best Practice Guidelines for Immunization)
CDC recommends pneumococcal vaccination for all adults 50 and older. Older adults are at greatest risk of serious pneumococcal illness.
